claim: KCNQ1 (Kv7.1) is a voltage-gated K+ channel whose gating behavior depends mainly on its auxiliary subunit KCNE proteins.
source: KCNQ1 (Kv7.1) is a voltage-gated K+ channel. Its gating behavior depends mainly on its auxiliary subunit KCNE proteins (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: There are five KCNE genes in the human genome.
source: There are five KCNE genes in the human genome, and all of them are known to modify KCNQ1 channel gating behavior, at least in Xenopus oocytes or mammalian cell lines (Bendahhou et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bendahhou et al., 2005.

claim: All five KCNE genes modify KCNQ1 channel gating behavior in Xenopus oocytes or mammalian cell lines.
source: There are five KCNE genes in the human genome, and all of them are known to modify KCNQ1 channel gating behavior, at least in Xenopus oocytes or mammalian cell lines (Bendahhou et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bendahhou et al., 2005.

claim: The cardiac KCNQ1-KCNE1 channel underlies the slow cardiac delayed-rectifier K+ current (IKs).
source: The most well-studied example is the cardiac KCNQ1-KCNE1 channel, which underlies the slow cardiac delayed-rectifier K+ current (IKs) (Barhanin et al., 1996; Sanguinetti et al., 1996; Takumi et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barhanin et al., 1996; Sanguinetti et al., 1996; Takumi et al., 1988.

claim: The KCNQ1-KCNE3 channel is a constitutively open channel expressed in epithelial cells in the trachea, stomach, and intestine.
source: Another example is the KCNQ1-KCNE3 channel, a constitutively open channel expressed in epithelial cells in the trachea, stomach, and intestine.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The KCNQ1-KCNE3 channel complex couples with some ion transporters to facilitate ion transport by recycling K+.
source: This channel complex couples with some ion transporters to facilitate ion transport by recycling K+ (Abbott, 2016; Grahammer et al., 2001; Preston et al., 2010; Schroeder et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abbott, 2016; Grahammer et al., 2001; Preston et al., 2010; Schroeder et al., 2000.

claim: KCNQ1 is a classic shaker-type tetrameric voltage-gated K+ channel with four independent voltage sensor domains (VSDs).
source: Since KCNQ1 is a classic shaker-type tetrameric voltage-gated K+ channel, it has four independent voltage sensor domains (VSDs), one from each α subunit (Long et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Long et al., 2005.

claim: Each VSD consists of four transmembrane segments, S1–S4.
source: Each VSD consists of four transmembrane segments, S1–S4.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Each S4 segment bears several positively charged amino acid residues.
source: Each S4 segment bears several positively charged amino acid residues.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: When the membrane potential is depolarized, each S4 segment moves upward (toward the extracellular side).
source: When the membrane potential is depolarized, each S4 segment moves upward (toward the extracellular side). That upward movement eventually triggers pore opening (Jensen et al., 2012; Larsson et al., 1996; Mannuzzu et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2012; Larsson et al., 1996; Mannuzzu et al., 1996.

claim: The upward movement of the S4 segment eventually triggers pore opening.
source: When the membrane potential is depolarized, each S4 segment moves upward (toward the extracellular side). That upward movement eventually triggers pore opening (Jensen et al., 2012; Larsson et al., 1996; Mannuzzu et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2012; Larsson et al., 1996; Mannuzzu et al., 1996.

claim: The S4 segment is considered to be an essential part of voltage sensing.
source: Therefore, the S4 segment is considered to be an essential part of voltage sensing (Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996; Catterall, 1988; Fedida and Hesketh, 2001; Liman et al., 1991; Logothetis et al., 1992; Noda et al., 1984; Papazian et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996; Catterall, 1988; Fedida and Hesketh, 2001; Liman et al., 1991; Logothetis et al., 1992; Noda et al., 1984; Papazian et al., 1991.

claim: The S4 segment of the KCNQ1 channel moves upward with depolarization, as proved by scanning cysteine accessibility mutagenesis.
source: As in the Shaker K+ channel, the S4 segment of the KCNQ1 channel also moves upward with depolarization, as proved by scanning cysteine accessibility mutagenesis (Nakajo and Kubo, 2007; Rocheleau and Kobertz, 2008) and voltage-clamp fluorometry (VCF; Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Nakajo and Kubo, 2014; Osteen et al., 2012; Osteen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nakajo and Kubo, 2007; Rocheleau and Kobertz, 2008.

claim: The S4 segment of the KCNQ1 channel moves upward with depolarization, as proved by voltage-clamp fluorometry (VCF).
source: As in the Shaker K+ channel, the S4 segment of the KCNQ1 channel also moves upward with depolarization, as proved by scanning cysteine accessibility mutagenesis (Nakajo and Kubo, 2007; Rocheleau and Kobertz, 2008) and voltage-clamp fluorometry (VCF; Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Nakajo and Kubo, 2014; Osteen et al., 2012; Osteen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Nakajo and Kubo, 2014; Osteen et al., 2012; Osteen et al., 2010.

claim: The presence of KCNE proteins affects the voltage sensor movement.
source: In those studies, the presence of KCNE proteins was found to affect the voltage sensor movement.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text, referring to previous studies.

claim: KCNE proteins stabilize a specific state during the voltage sensor transition.
source: These results suggest that KCNE proteins stabilize a specific state during the voltage sensor transition (Barro-Soria et al., 2017; Barro-Soria et al., 2015; Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Nakajo, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barro-Soria et al., 2017; Barro-Soria et al., 2015; Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Nakajo, 2019.

claim: There are at least three positions in the VSDs of KCNQ1: 'down,' 'intermediate,' and 'up'.
source: There should be at least three positions in the VSDs of KCNQ1: 'down,' 'intermediate,' and 'up' (Hou et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hou et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2020.

claim: KCNE1 stabilizes the intermediate position of VSDs along with a direct interaction of the pore domain and inhibits opening of the pore domain.
source: KCNE1 stabilizes the intermediate position of VSDs along with a direct interaction of the pore domain and inhibits opening of the pore domain (Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2020.

claim: KCNE3 may stabilize the intermediate or up position of VSDs and indirectly stabilize the channel's open state.
source: In contrast, KCNE3 may stabilize the intermediate or up position of VSDs and indirectly stabilize the channel's open state (Barro-Soria et al., 2017; Barro-Soria et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barro-Soria et al., 2017; Barro-Soria et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2020.

claim: 'The triplet' of amino acid residues in the middle of the transmembrane segment ('FTL': F57-T58-L59 in KCNE1 and 'TVG': T71-V72-G73 in KCNE3) are structural determinants of KCNE modulation properties.
source: Early studies by Melman et al. revealed 'the triplet' of amino acid residues in the middle of the transmembrane segment ('FTL': F57-T58-L59 in KCNE1 and 'TVG': T71-V72-G73 in KCNE3) as structural determinants of KCNE modulation properties (Melman et al., 2002; Melman et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Melman et al., 2002; Melman et al., 2001.

claim: Exchanging the triplet (or one of the three amino acid residues) between KCNE1 and KCNE3 could introduce the other's modulation properties, at least partially.
source: Exchanging the triplet (or one of the three amino acid residues) between KCNE1 and KCNE3 could introduce the other's modulation properties, at least partially.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text, referring to previous studies.

claim: Introducing 'FTL' into KCNE3 transforms it into a KCNE1-like protein.
source: For example, introducing 'FTL' into KCNE3 transforms it into a KCNE1-like protein.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as an example.

claim: Possible interaction sites of the KCNQ1 side are believed to be located between the pore domain and the VSD.
source: Possible interaction sites of the KCNQ1 side have also been explored and are believed to be located between the pore domain and the VSD (Chung et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2008; Nakajo and Kubo, 2007; Van Horn et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2008; Nakajo and Kubo, 2007; Van Horn et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2008.

claim: F127 and F130 of the S1 segment are required for KCNE3 to make KCNQ1 a constitutively open channel.
source: By utilizing the KCNQ1 ortholog from ascidian Ciona intestinalis, which lacks KCNE genes, we previously found that F127 and F130 of the S1 segment are required for KCNE3 to make KCNQ1 a constitutively open channel (Nakajo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakajo et al., 2011.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the KCNQ1-KCNE3-calmodulin complex shows that KCNE3 interacts with the S1 segment and the pore domain.
source: A recent computational model and the cryo-EM structure of the KCNQ1-KCNE3-calmodulin (CaM) complex clearly showed that KCNE3 interacts with the S1 segment and the pore domain (Kroncke et al., 2016; Sun and MacKinnon, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kroncke et al., 2016; Sun and MacKinnon, 2020.

claim: The side chains of seven amino acid residues in the S1 segment of KCNQ1 (F123, F127, F130, L134, I138, L142, and I145) face lining those of six amino acid residues of the KCNE3 transmembrane segment (S57, I61, M65, A69, G73, and I76).
